rules.h1sub: Card game rules & how to play
rules.setupLead: You need a standard 52-card deck without jokers and 2 to 5 players. A round takes only a few minutes.
rules.dealP: Shuffle and deal 4 cards face down to each player. Without looking, everyone arranges their cards in a square of two rows in front of them.
rules.setupAlt: In the middle lie the face-down draw pile and the face-up discard pile. In front of the player, four face-down cards in a square; the two nearest ones have been looked at.
rules.lgPeekS: at the two cards nearest to you
rules.setupP: Put the rest of the deck in the middle as the draw pile and turn its top card over to start the discard pile. Then everyone secretly looks at the two cards nearest to them – once only – and puts them back in place. From now on, memory is all you have.
rules.valLead: Every card counts as many points as its number. Low cards are good, high cards are bad.
rules.valP: Ace = 1, Jack = 11, Queen = 12. Kings are special: the black kings are the worst cards at 13 points, the red kings are the best at 0 points. Suits don’t matter otherwise.
rules.turnLead: In the first round any player starts; after that, whoever had the lowest total in the previous round starts. Play goes clockwise. On your turn you take exactly one card – or you call “Cabo” instead (see Cabo!).
rules.dq: Where do you take your card from?
rules.bStockP: Look at the card without showing it. Then choose:
rules.bStock1: Swap it for one of your cards: the new card goes face down in its place, the old one face up onto the discard pile.
rules.bStock2: Discard it face up. If it’s a 7 to queen, you may use its power now.
rules.bDiscP: Take the top card. You must swap it for one of your cards – the old card goes onto the discard pile. Powers don’t count here.
rules.dnext: Then it’s the next player’s turn.
rules.multiP: Do you think two or more of your cards have the same rank, for example two 5s? Then you can swap all of them for the one new card (whether from the draw or discard pile). Turn them face up: if they really match, they all go onto the discard pile and the new card takes one of their places. You now have fewer cards – great for your total.
rules.multiAlt: A drawn 2 replaces two 5s from your own cards at once.
rules.multiFail: If one card doesn’t match, you were wrong: turn the cards face down again in their places and add the new card face down to your cards as a penalty.
rules.memP: You may only look at your face-down cards with a power. Leave every card where it lies, so you and everyone else can keep track of what is where.
rules.powLead: The cards from 7 to queen have a power. You may only use it if you drew the card from the draw pile and discard it right away. Using the power is your whole turn.
rules.pow7p: Look at one of your own face-down cards, then put it back.
rules.pow9p: Look at one card of another player. Only you see it.
rules.powJp: Swap any two cards on the table – yours or other players’ – without looking at them. Everyone sees where they go.
rules.powKp: Kings can’t do anything. A black king is best discarded straight away, a red king is best kept.
rules.powRhyme: A rhyme to remember: seven, eight – check your plate; nine, ten – peek at a friend; jack, queen – swap unseen.
rules.caboLead: Once you think you have the lowest total at the table, you can end the round.
rules.c1p: At the start of your turn, instead of taking a card, say “Cabo”. That’s your whole turn.
rules.c2h: One last turn for everyone else
rules.c2p: Each other player has one more normal turn. You don’t play any more, though the others may still spy on or swap your cards during their last turn.
rules.c3p: Now everyone turns all their cards face up and adds up the points.
rules.caboEmpty: If the draw pile runs out before anyone calls “Cabo”, the round ends at once and is scored the same way – without a caller.
rules.scoreLead: After every round, write down the points. They add up from round to round.
rules.score1: Everyone scores the total of their cards.
rules.score2: The caller scores 0 if they have the lowest total, or share it.
rules.score3: Is someone lower than the caller? Then the caller scores their total plus 10 penalty points.
rules.exP: Mia has 6 points (the red king counts 0), Ben has 12. Mia is lowest, so she scores 0. Had Ben had only 5 points, Mia would have scored 6 + 10 = 16.
rules.endP: Keep playing rounds until someone goes over 100 points. The game ends then, and the player with the lowest total wins. Hit exactly 100? Lucky you: your score drops to 50 – but only once per game.
rules.varLead: Cabo is played in many ways. Agree before the first round which of these rules you use:
rules.var1: Only one king at 0: Only the king of diamonds (the “one-eyed king”) counts 0; the other three kings count 13.
rules.var2: Simpler swap: With a jack or queen you always swap one of your own cards with a card of another player.
rules.var3: Older scoring: The lowest player always scores 0, even without calling. A caller who isn’t lowest only gets 5 penalty points instead of 10.
rules.var4: Other start: Look at any two of your cards instead of the two nearest – or only at one, for a harder game.
rules.var5: Throw in at any time: As soon as a card lands on the discard pile, anyone who has a card of the same rank may throw it on top. A wrong guess costs a penalty card. This rule is typical of Cambio.
rules.var6: Empty draw pile: Instead of ending the round, shuffle the discard pile (except its top card) and keep playing.
rules.var7: With jokers: Add the two jokers; they count 0 points and have no power.
rules.var8: Kamikaze: Whoever finishes the round with two queens and two black kings (two 12s and two 13s) scores 0 points – and everyone else scores 50.
rules.faq1q: Can I look at my cards again later?
rules.faq1a: No. After the start, you only see your own cards with a 7 or 8 – or when you discard them. Everything else you have to remember.
rules.faq2q: Can I use a power if I take the card from the discard pile?
rules.faq2a: No. Powers only work with cards from the draw pile that you discard straight away. From the discard pile you always have to swap.
rules.faq3q: Can I keep a 7 instead of using its power?
rules.faq3a: Yes. Then you simply swap it for one of your cards, and it counts 7 points at the end like any other card.
rules.faq4a: There is no fixed rule. If you are fairly sure you have only a few points – around 5 or less – it is often a good moment. But remember the 10 penalty points if someone else is lower.
rules.faq5q: What happens if a player has no cards left?
rules.faq5a: In the basic Cabo rules you always keep at least one card, because a new card replaces the ones you swap out. If you play with the house rule Throw in at any time and end up with no cards left, your total is 0 – you can’t go any lower, so you are hard to beat in that round.
rules.faq6q: Is Cabo the same as Cambio?
rules.faq6a: They are close relatives. The idea is the same, and the game is also known as Pablo or Cactus. The details differ from table to table – Cambio, for example, usually lets everyone throw matching cards onto the discard pile at any time (see Variants).
rules.faq7a: Yes, Cabo also exists as a commercial card game with its own deck, created in 2010 by Melissa Limes and Mandy Henning. This page explains how to play with a standard deck of cards.
rules.sheetCta: Keep score with the free online score sheet: it adds up the rounds and applies the penalty for you.

info.gearAlt: A standard deck of 52 playing cards
info.intro: Cabo is a brisk memory card game where your four cards stay face down and you only see them for a moment. Swap smartly, keep track of the table and call Cabo before anyone else beats your score – all with a regular deck of cards.

goal: The goal: End each round with the lowest total of points in front of you. The catch: your four cards lie face down, and you only know them if you remember them.

strategy.sub: Memory, timing and smart swaps. Cabo is easy to learn, yet knowing when to peek, when to ignore the discard pile and when to call “Cabo” wins far more rounds than lucky draws.
strategy.principle: Cabo is a race for information and low totals. Every card you know is an advantage, every unknown card is a hidden risk – and shrinking your hand from four cards to three beats almost any single swap.
principleItems: Information first, points second. Early in the round, turning unknown back-row cards into known low cards matters more than shaving a single point off a card you already know.
Fewer cards win rounds. A clean multi-swap drops your hand from four cards to three (or two), cutting your total permanently.
Silence is information too. Never give away your hand by taking middling cards from the discard pile or reacting when you draw a red king.
strategy.memLead: With four face-down cards – and other players spying and swapping – a simple mental habit stops your cards from blurring together.
strategy.memExH: Read your square like a 4-digit code
strategy.memExAlt: Four cards in a 2 by 2 square: two unknown cards at the back, 4 of hearts and 9 of spades in front, read as ? ? 4 9. After swapping a drawn 2 of diamonds into the top-left spot, the code updates to 2 ? 4 9.
strategy.memExWhy: Why? Always read your square in the exact same order – top left, top right, bottom left, bottom right – and repeat the four slots silently after every change. A single updated digit sticks much better than four separate pictures.
memItems: Repeat the code between turns. Whenever you swap or peek, silently run through all four positions once right away.

Replace unknowns before known medium cards. Drew a 2? Put it on an unknown back-row spot (or a known 10+) rather than overwriting a known 4 – that reveals the unknown card on the discard pile for free.
Track one spot per opponent. You don’t need to memorize the whole table. Just remember where someone placed a red king, ace or 2 from the discard pile so you have a ready target for a jack or queen.
strategy.drawLead: Where you take your card tells the table almost as much as what you discard.
drawItems: Be picky with the discard pile. Taking a face-up card lets everyone see its exact value and where you put it. Only take from the discard pile for a red king (0), ace (1), 2 or 3 – or to complete a multi-swap.

Use clear swap thresholds. From the draw pile, swap 0 to 3 into an unknown spot; swap 4 or 5 only over a known 8 or higher. Cards from 7 to queen are usually worth more for their power unless they replace a black king (13) or queen (12).
Watch what opponents pick up. Whenever another player grabs a low card from the discard pile, lock in that spot – it’s free information without spending a 9 or 10.
strategy.drawWarn: Don’t grab a 4 or 5 from the discard pile just because you dislike an unknown card: you tell the whole table where your 4 sits and give up the chance to draw a lower card or a power.
strategy.powLead: Powers only work when drawn from the draw pile and discarded at once – make every one count.
strategy.pow7h: 7 or 8 – Peek at your blind spots first
strategy.pow7p: Always look at your two unknown back-row cards before re-checking anything else. Once an opponent uses a jack or queen on one of your spots, peek there immediately so a hidden 12 or 13 doesn’t ruin your call.
strategy.pow9p: Spy on the player with the fewest cards or on a spot they haven’t replaced all round (often a 0, 1 or 2). Don’t waste a spy on a card you already watched them take from the discard pile.
strategy.powJh: Jack or queen – Swap with intel, not blind luck
strategy.powJp: Remember you can swap any two cards on the table. Best move: trade your known high card (10–13) for an opponent’s known low card – or disrupt the “Cabo” caller on your final turn by swapping their best card away.
strategy.powKh: Red king vs. black king – Keep a poker face
strategy.powKp: Discard a drawn black king (13) straight away. When you draw a red king (0), swap it smoothly into an unknown or high spot without smiling – if nobody notices, it’s far less likely to get stolen.
strategy.multiLead: Two rules in Cabo create huge swings if you plan for them.
multiItems: Prioritize multi-swaps early. Even trading two 5s (10 points) for a drawn 6 cuts four points immediately and drops you to three cards – from there you are one swap away from calling “Cabo”.
Never guess a multi-swap. A wrong match costs you an extra face-down card on top of keeping the old ones. Only attempt it when you are 100 % sure of every spot.

Play for exact 100 when behind. Sitting at 88–97 points across rounds? Hitting exactly 100 drops you straight back to 50 (once per game) – sometimes keeping one extra card or avoiding a risky call is worth aiming for that exact total.
strategy.callLead: Calling too early risks +10 penalty points; calling too late lets everyone else catch up and swap your cards.
callItems: Remember: your cards are NOT locked. During their last turn, other players can still spy on or swap your cards with a jack or queen. Calling around 4–6 points early, while opponents still have unknowns, is often safer than waiting for 1–2 points.
Know every card before calling. Calling with an unknown spot is a gamble: a single hidden black king turns a 3-point hand into 16 plus 10 penalty points.
Ties go to the caller. You score 0 even if someone ties your lowest total – so if you hold 3–4 points and nobody has multi-swapped down to two cards, call confidently.
Read the table’s card counts. If an opponent is already down to two cards, expect a total around 3–6 and only call “Cabo” if you can match or beat it.
mistakes: Taking medium cards (4–6) from the discard pile. You show everyone what you took and give up a blind draw that could be a 0–3 or a useful power.
Swapping over a known card while unknowns remain. Putting a 2 on a known 5 leaves your back row blind – replace an unknown card first to learn what was hiding there.
Forgetting a swapped spot. As soon as someone hits your square with a jack or queen, treat that spot as unknown again until you peek or replace it.
Blindly using jack or queen without a target. Swapping two random cards helps your opponent as often as it helps you – wait for discard intel or a 9/10 spy.
Gambling on an uncertain multi-swap. Adding a fifth penalty card almost guarantees a rough round.
Calling “Cabo” with an unknown card still face down. One hidden face card plus the 10-point penalty can swing the score by over 20 points.

quick.rule: 4 cards face down, peek at the 2 nearest once. Draw 1 (swap face-down or discard & use power) or take the top discard (must swap, no power). Lowest total wins.
quick.powNote: Powers only count when drawn from the draw pile and discarded right away.
quick.multi: Multi-swap: trade 2+ matching own cards for 1 new card (fewer cards!). Wrong = keep all + 1 penalty card.
quick.cabo: Call “Cabo”: instead of drawing; everyone else gets 1 last turn (may still swap yours). Lowest/tie = 0, beaten = sum + 10.
quick.score: Game over: past 100 points (lowest overall wins). Exact 100 drops to 50 (once).
